parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State the conditions required for the formation of a stationary wave.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what must meet and overlap to make a stationary pattern - a single travelling wave just carries energy away, so what second wave is needed?
Hint 2: For a stable pattern with fixed nodes, what must be identical about the two overlapping waves, and in which directions must they travel?
parts.proper_answer: Two progressive waves of the same frequency (same wavelength and speed) and same amplitude travelling in opposite directions superpose.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What a stationary wave really is**
You are used to a travelling wave carrying energy along. A stationary wave looks still, with fixed nodes and antinodes. That can only happen if energy is not flowing away in one direction.

Step 2: **Building it from two travelling waves**
Imagine a wave going right and an identical wave going left. Where they meet they add by superposition. Using $$v = f\lambda$$ both must have the same $f$, $\lambda$ and $v$ in the same medium, and ideally the same amplitude, so that at some points they always cancel to give nodes and at others they always reinforce to give antinodes.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
The sound from a loudspeaker is detected by a microphone that is connected to a cathode-ray oscilloscope (c.r.o.). Fig. 4.1 shows the trace on the screen of the c.r.o.

{{figure:figure_4_1}}

Fig. 4.1

In air, the sound wave has a speed of $330 \text{m s}^{-1}$ and a wavelength of $0.18 \text{m}$.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of the sound wave.
hints: Hint 1: You are given speed $v$ in air and wavelength $\lambda$ for the sound - which universal wave relation links $v$, $f$ and $\lambda$?
Hint 2: Check units are already SI ($\text{m s}^{-1}$ and $\text{m}$) so you can rearrange directly for $f$ and calculate in $\text{Hz}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose the governing law**
For any progressive wave the speed is set by how many wavelengths pass per second: $$v = f\lambda$$ Here $v = 330\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $\lambda = 0.18\text{ m}$.

Step 2: **Rearrange and calculate**
$$f = \frac{v}{\lambda} = \frac{330}{0.18}$$ $$f \approx 1830\text{ Hz} \approx 1.8\times 10^{3}\text{ Hz}$$ Keep 2 or 3 significant figures.

Hint 2: Check units are already SI ($\text{m s}^{-1}$ and $\text{m}$) so you can rearrange directly for $f$ and calculate in $\text{Hz}$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Determine the time-base setting, in $\text{s cm}^{-1}$, of the c.r.o.
hints: Hint 1: The time-base tells you how much time each horizontal cm represents. First find the time for one full cycle from your answer to (b)(i) using $T = 1/f$.
Hint 2: On Fig. 4.1 measure the horizontal length of one complete sine wave in cm (peak to next peak), then divide the period by that length.
parts.proper_answer: Period $T = 1/1830 \approx 5.5 \times 10^{-4}\text{ s}$. One cycle $\approx 8.0\text{ cm}$ on screen, so time-base $\approx 5.5\times 10^{-4}/8.0 \approx 6.8 \times 10^{-5}\text{ s cm}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Get the time for one oscillation**
From (b)(i) $f \approx 1.83\times 10^{3}\text{ Hz}$. $$T = \frac{1}{f} \approx \frac{1}{1830} \approx 5.5\times 10^{-4}\text{ s}$$ This is the real time of one sine wave you see.

Step 2: **Convert screen distance to time**
Measure peak-to-peak horizontal distance on Fig. 4.1. It is about $8.0\text{ cm}$ for one full $\lambda$. Time-base setting is time per cm: $$\text{time-base} = \frac{T}{\text{length of one cycle}} \approx \frac{5.5\times 10^{-4}}{8.0} \approx 6.8\times 10^{-5}\text{ s cm}^{-1}$$ The method earns credit even if your cm reading differs slightly.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text:
The intensity of the sound from the loudspeaker is now halved. The wavelength of the sound is unchanged. Assume that the amplitude of the trace is proportional to the amplitude of the sound wave.

On Fig. 4.1, sketch the new trace shown on the screen of the c.r.o.
hints: Hint 1: Wavelength is unchanged, so what stays the same on the trace - the horizontal spacing or the height? Think about what frequency controls.
Hint 2: Intensity $I$ is proportional to (amplitude)$^2$. If $I$ halves, does amplitude halve? Work out the factor $1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.71$ for the new height.
parts.proper_answer: Same period / same horizontal positions, with reduced peak height about 0.71 of original. Intensity $\propto A^{2}$ so $A_{new}=A/\sqrt{2}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Keep the timing the same**
Wavelength and speed are unchanged, so $f$ is unchanged. Your sketch must have peaks and troughs at the same horizontal positions as Fig. 4.1.

Step 2: **Reduce the amplitude correctly**
For a wave, $$I \propto A^{2}$$ Halving $I$ gives: $$A_{new} = \frac{A_{old}}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.71 A_{old}$$ So draw the same sine shape but about 70 percent as tall, centred on the same line. A common mistake is to halve the height - that would quarter the intensity.

parts.label: (c)
(c)(i)
parts.text: Calculate the vertical distance between level A and level B.
hints: Hint 1: Loud sound means resonance - a stationary wave fits in the air column. Think how much longer the air column must get to fit the next resonance.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Successive resonances**
Level A is the first resonance where the air length is $\lambda/4$. The next loud point is when the length is $3\lambda/4$. The increase is: $$\Delta L = 3\lambda/4 - \lambda/4 = \lambda/2$$ So $$\Delta L = 0.18/2 = 0.090\text{ m}$$

enrichment.label: (c)(i)
key_concepts: successive loud positions separated by lambda/2
hints: Hint 1: Loud sound means resonance - a stationary wave fits in the air column. Think how much longer the air column must get to fit the next resonance.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Successive resonances**

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: On Fig. 4.3, label with the letter N the positions of the nodes of the stationary wave that is formed in the air column when the liquid surface is at level B.
hints: Hint 1: Remember where air cannot move - at the liquid surface (closed end) there must be a node, and at the open top there is an antinode.
parts.proper_answer: Label N at the liquid surface (level B) and a second N $\lambda/2$ ($0.09\text{ m}$) above it in the air column.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Where nodes sit**
You have an open-closed tube. The liquid is a hard boundary so displacement is zero there - a node N. The top is open - an antinode. When the length is $3\lambda/4$ there are two nodes: one at the surface at level B, and one half a wavelength above it, i.e. $0.090\text{ m}$ higher up the tube.

parts.label: (c)(iii)
parts.text:
The mass of liquid leaving the tube per unit time is $6.7 \text{g s}^{-1}$. The tube has an internal cross-sectional area of $13 \text{cm}^{2}$. The density of the liquid is $0.79 \text{g cm}^{-3}$.

Calculate the time taken for the liquid to move from level A to level B.
hints: Hint 1: First find the volume of liquid lost between A and B from the tube area and your distance from (c)(i). Remember to keep cm and m consistent.
Hint 2: Convert that volume to mass using density $\rho = m/V$, then use the mass loss rate to get time $t = m / (m/t)$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Volume then mass between A and B**
Distance $h = 0.090\text{ m} = 9.0\text{ cm}$. $$V = A h = 13 \times 9.0 = 117\text{ cm}^{3}$$ $$m = \rho V = 0.79 \times 117 \approx 92\text{ g}$$

Step 2: **Time from flow rate**
Mass leaves at $6.7\text{ g s}^{-1}$: $$t = \frac{m}{\text{rate}} = \frac{92.4}{6.7} \approx 13.8\text{ s} \approx 14\text{ s}$$
